Syllabic lateral affricate [tɬ] — one sound with no English equivalent, the tongue pressed to the palate.

pronunciation.approximation: 'METZ-tlee' — the stress falls on the first syllable, and 'tl' is a single sound: tongue pressed to the palate, air escaping at the sides.

pronunciation.note: Metztli is Tier 2: the registered form preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter — a mechanical fact, not a judgment. Classical Nahuatl had a long vowel (mētztli), which philological editions mark with a macron; the lexicon's canonical form carries the plain vowels, so the restoration stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: Metztli
domains.subtitle: Moon
domains.lead: Metztli is the Nahuatl moon — the word means both 'moon' and 'month,' so she is the sky's registrar of time. Colonial sources give the moon several faces: the dimmed twin Tecciztecatl, the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, and Metztli herself, the calm counting presence over night, calendar, and the moist arts of healing.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The Nahuatl word names the moon and the month at once — the sky's light and the calendar's unit in a single breath.

cards.name: Moon
cards.desc: The lunar disk governed the eighteen festival months of the veintena year and the night's vigil alike.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Kept alive in Nahuatl speech, the temazcal sweatbath, and the rabbit the whole world can still see on the moon's face.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Held as a Unicode domain temple so the moon's name keeps its scholarly form rather than a compromise.

symbols.name: The rabbit on the moon
symbols.meaning: The silhouette cast when a rival's too-bright moon was struck by a hurled rabbit; every Nahua child's explanation of the moon's face.

symbols.name: The lunar disk
symbols.meaning: The moon carried on the back of night-lords in codices; the disk itself is the deity's body.

symbols.name: Golden bells (coyolli)
symbols.meaning: The cheek-bells of Coyolxauhqui, 'She of the Golden Bells,' whose broken body is the moon as defeated rival.

symbols.name: The month
symbols.meaning: Metztli means moon and month alike; in Nahuatl the word is the calendar.

symbols.name: Bath steam
symbols.meaning: The vapour of the temazcal — the moon's moist light brought down into the house of healing and birth.

mythology.lead: The stories told of the Nahua moon are stories about light that must be limited: a twin who shines too bright and is struck by a rabbit, a sister dismembered at the serpent mountain, and a calm disk that keeps the months. The sources disagree about names — Tecciztecatl, Coyolxauhqui, Metztli herself — and the disagreement is the theology: one moon, many meanings.

myths.title: The Leap into the Fire
myths.text: At the dawn of the fifth era the gods assembled at Teotihuacan, and darkness still covered the world. Two volunteers offered themselves to become the lights. Nanahuatzin, the pustule-covered, leapt first into the sacred fire without hesitation; Tecciztecatl, the proud and bejewelled, flinched four times before at last following. The Codex Chimalpopoca's Leyenda de los Soles tells what happened: the humble one rose as the sun, and the splendid one rose as the moon, shining as bright as the day. The gods would not endure two equal lights. One of them seized a rabbit and hurled it into Tecciztecatl's face, dimming his splendour and fixing the dark silhouette on his disk. Sahagún's informants repeat the tale in the Florentine Codex (Book VII), where the moon's brightness is cut back precisely because the world needs contrast — day to work, night to fear and dream. The rabbit flew, the moon dimmed, and the celestial order was set. The myth means that in the Nahua cosmos even glory must accept a wound to become useful: the moon is what remains when a radiant rival is struck down to size.

myths.title: The Dismembered Sister
myths.text: On the serpent mountain of Coatepec, Coatlicue was sweeping when a ball of feathers descended upon her; she conceived, and her four hundred sons, led by Coyolxauhqui — 'She of the Golden Bells' — raged at the shame. As she attacked her mother, Huitzilopochtli sprang fully armed from Coatlicue's womb and cut his sister to pieces, hurling her head into the sky. The Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex (Book III) agree on the essentials, and the Coyolxauhqui Stone, excavated at the Templo Mayor in 1978, shows her broken body with bells on her cheeks — a moon dismembered by a sun. Scholars caution that the sources never simply call Coyolxauhqui 'Metztli'; rather, Nahua thought distributes the moon among several names. For the city that kept the sun's temple, the myth was political theology: the moon's light is the light of a defeated enemy, hung in the sky as a permanent warning. The myth means the moon is remembered violence — the night ruled by what the day dismembered.

myths.title: One Moon, Many Names
myths.text: The honest difficulty of Nahua lunar theology is that the colonial sources disagree. Sahagún gives Tecciztecatl the leap into the fire; the Coatepec myth gives Coyolxauhqui the dismembered head; the day-counts and ritual orations preserve Metztli simply as the moon and the month; and the night is ruled by Yohualtecuhtli, 'Lord of Night,' often shown with the lunar disk on his back. Seler's comparative studies treated these as overlapping masks of a single lunar complex, while Nicholson's survey of central Mexican religion lists them as distinct personalities the Mexica themselves never systematized into one lunar theology. The Mexica, it seems, did not feel the need for one moon. What unites the names is function: the moon counts the month, so whoever wears the disk is time's registrar. The mythological lesson is that a culture can hold several contradictory stories about the same light without anxiety — the moon as rival, as dimmed twin, as calendar — because what matters is not the name but the counting.

myths.title: Grandmother of the Bath
myths.text: Closely woven into the lunar sphere is Temazcalteci, 'Grandmother of the Sweatbath,' whom Sahagún's informants praise in the Florentine Codex (Book VI) as patroness of the temazcal, of medicinal herbs, and of women in childbirth — a goddess whose steam, like the moon's, is a vapour that heals. The sweatbath was a sacred precinct served by midwives and its own deity, and later scholarship from Seler onward has linked the bathhouse, with its night hours, its water, and its female arts, to the wider lunar world to which Metztli gives her name. The connection should be stated carefully: no colonial text calls Temazcalteci 'Metztli'. But the logic of the pairing is old — moon, water, steam, and the arts of healing travel together across Mesoamerica, and the Maya codices give their moon goddess Ix Chel the same portfolio of weaving and medicine. The myth means that the moon's domain is not only the sky: it is the bath, the womb, the herb, and the hour that counts the labor of birth.

lore.syncretism: Under Spanish rule the moon's cult did not end but changed costume. The Immaculata stands on a crescent, and the Virgin of Guadalupe keeps lunar imagery in her mantle's folds. Maya parallels — Ix Chel of the Dresden and Madrid codices — kept the same lunar triangle of weaving, healing, and flood that the Nahua sources distribute across Metztli, Temazcalteci, and the moon-rabbit. In the bilingual centuries metztli became the Spanish word's quiet rival: luna names the body, metztli names the reckoning. Modern Nahuatl speakers still say metztli for both moon and month, and Mexican folklore still points out the rabbit on the moon's face. The syncretism is less a conquest than a translation: the Virgin inherits the crescent; the rabbit keeps the disk.
lore.culturalLegacy: Metztli survives first in language: in modern Nahuatl, metztli still means both moon and month — one of the oldest living double meanings in the Americas. The twenty day-signs of the tonalpohualli and the eighteen veintena months kept lunar time central to Mexica civic life, and Durán describes whole cities reordering themselves around each new fire and new month. The temazcal — the sweatbath overseen by the lunar healer Temazcalteci — remains in use across Mexico and the diaspora. In popular culture the rabbit on the moon is told to children to this day, and the name circulates in art, poetry, and identity movements that reclaim Nahuatl heritage. The moon in Mexico is not a dead myth but a working word: to say metztli is still to count the month.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Metztli's deepest lesson is lodged in grammar. In Nahuatl the same word names the light in the sky and the interval it measures — moon is month. The Mexica did not divide the luminous object from the time it kept; the watcher and the clock were one being. That is a more intimate astronomy than ours. We have inherited a moon that has been weighed, mapped, and walked upon, and in exchange we have mostly lost the older moon — the one that told farmers when to plant, healers when to steam, and midwives when the month had turned.

The restoration of Metztli is thus more than a spelling: it is the return of a word that once made time personal. When several contradictory myths — a dimmed rival, a dismembered sister, a night-lord's burden — can all be true of the same pale disk, the culture is confessing that the moon exceeds any single story. Perhaps that is the mark of a genuinely living sky-myth: not that it resolves, but that it keeps counting.
lore.archaeology: Material evidence for the Nahua moon is anchored at the Templo Mayor: the Coyolxauhqui Stone (c. 1473, Phase II), a monolith some 3.25 metres across of the dismembered moon goddess, excavated by Eduardo Matos Moctezuma's team in 1978. Lunar deities carry the moon disk on their backs in codices such as the Codex Borgia and the Codex Fejérváry-Mayer. The textual evidence is equally material: Sahagún's Florentine Codex (Books I, III, VI, VII) was compiled 1555–1576 in Nahuatl and Spanish with Nahua elders, and the Codex Chimalpopoca preserves the Leyenda de los Soles — both manuscripts, not folklore collections, and the core witnesses for the leap into the fire and the rabbit hurled to dim the moon.
